content: When two users attempt to edit the same page simultaneously, an edit conflict occurs. For example, if Alice begins editing a page and saves her changes, and then Bob, who started editing the same page at the same time, tries to save his changes, Bob will encounter an edit conflict page. The edit conflict page is structured as follows: At the top, Alice's version of the entire page is displayed, even if Bob was only editing a specific section. At the bottom, Bob's intended changes are shown. This could be his version of the entire page or just the section he was editing. In the middle, a comparison (diff) of the two versions is presented. For the section Bob was editing, the diff highlights both Bob's and Alice's changes, except for identical modifications. For other sections, the diff shows the full new text as if it were entirely added. Bob can edit the upper text and save it. However, if Bob was editing only a section, saving without removing the other sections may result in duplication of content. This is considered a bug. The recommended approach is for Bob to save his changes elsewhere (e.g., copy them to the clipboard), cancel the edit, and try again. Occasionally, if the system is slow, a user may inadvertently create an edit conflict with themselves by attempting to save changes multiple times before the system processes the first save. In such cases, the upper text on the edit conflict page may not reflect the most recent changes. The system may process the earlier change in the background while the user is still viewing the edit conflict page, leading to discrepancies in the displayed text. To resolve an edit conflict: If Bob's changes are minor and Alice's are substantial, Bob may choose to work from Alice's version and reapply his changes. He might add a note like via edit conflict to inform Alice and others of the situation, allowing Alice to review the merge for accuracy. If Bob's changes are significant and Alice's are minor, Bob may choose to work from his version. He can copy his changes into the upper text, provide an appropriate edit summary (e.g., via edit conflict, will remerge), and then review the page history to identify and reapply Alice's changes in a subsequent edit. If both Alice and Bob made extensive changes, they should collaborate to determine the best way to merge their edits. For instance, if both added large sections on the same topic, Bob might save his changes, and then both can review the versions together to decide on the final content. Bob should not overwrite Alice's changes without consideration. It is essential to assume good faith and avoid overwriting others' edits out of carelessness or laziness. Logical edit conflicts, which are not detected by the system, can occur when someone copies the source text into an external editor, makes extensive changes, and then pastes the entire content back into the page. This can overwrite any changes made by others in the meantime. To prevent this, users should either paste their changes into the same edit box they originally copied from or check the page history for intervening edits and merge them before saving. Mistakes in the merging process are inevitable because humans are fallible. If Bob accidentally reverses some of Alice's changes, Alice should not revert the page to her version. Instead, she should edit Bob's version to reinstate her changes while preserving Bob's improvements. She can add an edit summary, such as Reinstating link which Bob accidentally removed, to clarify her actions. If Bob repeatedly makes the same error, Alice should address the issue on his talk page in a friendly manner, providing guidance on resolving edit conflicts. When reverting a page to a previous version, the edit conflict warning system is not triggered. This can unintentionally overwrite changes made in the meantime. To avoid this, users should copy the text from the old version into the latest version's edit box and check the diff before saving. Reversion wars should be avoided. To minimize edit conflicts, users can adopt certain practices: Edit pages that have not been recently modified. Make larger, less frequent edits rather than numerous small ones. Use the Show preview button to review changes before saving. Utilize the In Use template ({{inuse}}) to indicate that a page is being actively edited, removing it once the edits are complete. Wikipedia also includes a CVS-style edit conflict merging feature, which uses the diff3 utility to handle conflicts. This feature only triggers an edit conflict if users attempt to edit the same lines of text.
